name: Joseph Goebbels
role: Reich Minister of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda, Nazi Germany (1933–1945)
summary: Joseph Goebbels was Nazi Germany's propaganda minister and a senior party leader who wrote and spoke extensively for the regime. His surviving texts reject parliamentary democracy, Marxism and liberalism, call for one party under a single leader, and promote racial hierarchy, antisemitism and total war; from 1941 his articles called for the removal and destruction of Europe's Jews. Early in the 1920s he held socialist-leaning views that he dropped after 1926.

sources.title: Joseph Goebbels
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.usedFor: Career and positions: early Strasserite period and the 1926 break with it, Reich Chamber of Culture, 1933 book burning, Kristallnacht, the Sudeten and Polish campaigns, reported statements on the Protestant and Catholic churches, 1933 press and emergency decrees.

sources.title: Nazi Propaganda by Joseph Goebbels 1933-1945 (German Propaganda Archive, Calvin University, compiled by Randall Bytwerk; PDF of the speech and article collection)
sources.author: Joseph Goebbels (translated and edited by Randall Bytwerk)

(1941), 'England's Guilt' and 'The Coffee Drinkers' (1939), 'German Women' (1933), 'The Racial Question and World Propaganda' (1933), 'More Morality, Less Moralism' (1934), 'Youth and the War' (1940), Hitler-birthday speeches, New Year speeches 1934 and 1939, 'Immortal German Culture' (1943), 'Don't Be Too Fair!' (1942).

universal-healthcare.rationale: His 1939 'England's Guilt' article contrasts England's 'social welfare programs' that workers only hear about with German social policy. No statement on health coverage as such.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: In 1939 he calls capitalist democracy a system suffering from 'every possible modern social ailment' that exploits colonies. He does not defend market allocation as such.

public-ownership.rationale: He calls Germany 'a socialist people's state' (1939 'England's Guilt'). Nationalisation as a programme is not in the texts read, so the answer is low.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: The 1943 Sportpalast speech says 'Rich and poor, high and low must share the burdens equally' in the war effort. This is wartime burden-sharing rather than a tax rate.

unions-good.rationale: Wikipedia reports that trade unions were disbanded in 1933 and replaced by the German Labour Front. He is not recorded arguing for unions' value in the texts read.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: 'Don't Be Too Fair!' (1942) says Germans must be taught to hate, and his articles call for hostility toward Jews and enemies. He promoted hatred as propaganda rather than arguing for legal limits on it.

strong-leader.rationale: His Hitler-birthday speeches praise the Führer as the leader who acts where parliaments fail. He calls parliamentary politicians 'parliamentary mayflies' and says the Reich now rests on 'one man and one idea'.

state-harmful.rationale: In 1943 he treats the state as the instrument of the national community and calls for total state direction of life. He does not regard the state as unnecessary.

empower-police-military.rationale: 'Total War' (1943) demands full mobilisation and draconian penalties for shirkers, and his articles call the German army the only defence against Bolshevism. He supports military power and authority.

decide-locally.rationale: In the March 1933 speeches he says all propaganda and public information institutions are to be 'centralized in one hand', and Wikipedia says he ran the national Reich Chambers. He is not recorded favouring local decisions.

traditional-family.rationale: 'German Women' (1933) says the first, best and most suitable place for women is in the family, and that the family is the nation's source of strength.

abortion-legal.rationale: Inferred: The 1933 'German Women' speech blames the 'liberal attitude toward the family and the child' for Germany's decline. Inferred opposition to liberal family policy; abortion is not named.

more-religion-public.rationale: He invokes God and 'divine providence' in speeches yet attacks churches and clergy. Contested, so 0.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: The 1933 'Racial Question' speech says the racial problem will be solved only when the people act 'for their own good', and he rejects redressing wrongs done to Jews. He opposes correcting the position of groups he calls racial enemies.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: 'Immortal German Culture' (1943) and his speeches defend German culture and its two-thousand-year heritage against foreign influence. He treats national culture as worth preserving.

gradual-change.rationale: He describes the 1933 change as a national revolution that swept away parliamentary politics quickly, and calls it an act of renewal rather than gradual reform.

nation-first.rationale: His 1941-1945 articles put German national survival and interests first, and 'Total War' says the nation's cohesion must come before private interests.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Inferred: his 1939 propaganda framed the invasion of Poland as protecting Germans from persecution. Inferred from that framing, and a justification rather than a general statement.

revolution-justified.rationale: He calls the National Socialist takeover a 'national revolution' and a 'revolutionary government' while condemning the 1918 November revolution. He justifies revolution by its aims.

central-planning.rationale: In 'Total War' (1943) he describes the wartime conversion as following a plan. He never argues that planning beats markets in general.

state-directs-investment.rationale: The 1943 'Total War' speech describes the state directing labour and closing shops to free resources for armaments production, and says 'We are following a plan'.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: He drove the mandatory Reich Chamber of Culture (1933), whose sub-chambers controlled entry to each trade, and the Labour Front replaced unions. These are state-organised bodies, though not wage-setting bodies.

one-party-rule.rationale: In the 1933 'Racial Question' speech he says 'parliamentarianism and the party system are outdated concepts for us', and the Reich is governed by one movement. He endorses a single ruling party.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: In 'What would there be European about Europe' he praises 'German kaisers and kings, counts and generals' for withstanding attacks from the east. Partial praise of past monarchs, so low.

democracy-best.rationale: He calls parliamentary democracy and the party system 'outdated concepts' (1933) and mocks democracy as 'liberal-democratic phrases'. He does not regard democracy as the best government.

political-violence-never.rationale: The 1938 Nuremberg record of his remarks to party leaders reports the anti-Jewish demonstrations of November 1938 that party leaders were told to organise while appearing uninvolved, and his articles call for violence against enemies. He does not regard political violence as never justified.

war-builds-character.rationale: In one of his Hitler-birthday speeches he says war 'separates the strong from the weak' and that a people's character is tested by it. He sees war as strengthening.

separate-church-state.rationale: He attacks churches and clergy and wanted to eliminate the Protestant Church, yet invokes God and divine providence in his speeches. Contested, so 0.

military-superiority.rationale: 'Total War' (1943) and the 1941 'When or How?' article describe armed strength and the means of war as the nation's guarantee of survival. He supports military superiority.

ethnic-nation.rationale: The 1933 'Racial Question' speech and the 1941 'The Jews are Guilty' article define the German nation against Jews as a racial 'community' and call for removing Jews from it. He wants a nation of one people.

class-struggle-history.rationale: The 1934 New Year text dismisses 'the Marxist nonsense that had tortured the German people for six decades' and says a community of the people replaced it. He rejects class conflict as history's engine.

equal-outcomes.rationale: The 1933 'Racial Question' speech calls 'the insane belief in equality' a thing of the past. He rejects equality as a political aim but does not address equality of outcome specifically.

colonial-reparations.rationale: 'The Coffee Drinkers' (1939) and 'England's Guilt' say Britain grows rich by exploiting its colonies. He faults colonial powers for exploitation, though he does not state reparations.

civilizational-union.rationale: His 1941-1945 articles appeal to 'Western civilization' and European unity against Bolshevism, and call for a European order under German-led cooperation.

duties-before-rights.rationale: The 1933 'German Women' speech says women 'have been given more rights but fewer duties' and that this is a bad trade. He puts duty before individual rights.

limit-population.rationale: The 1933 'German Women' speech warns of falling births and demands more children to save the nation. He opposes limiting population.

profit-exploitation.rationale: In 1939 he accuses British capitalists of exploiting colonies and keeping workers in poverty. This attacks capitalist exploitation rather than stating the general claim about profit.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: His 1926 'Lenin or Hitler?' speech and 1930s articles describe Bolshevism as a terror of Jewish-led revolution. He opposes a proletarian dictatorship.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: He blames 'plutocratic' England and the United States for the war, but attributes it to British policy and Jewish interests rather than to capitalism's inner logic.

harm-principle.rationale: In 'More Morality, Less Moralism' (1934) he says the state should regulate the great moral foundations of national life but not the purely personal conduct of individuals. This is only a partial match to a harm principle.

individual-rights-only.rationale: The 1933 'Racial Question' speech rejects 'excessive individualism' and says the principle of personality serves the national community. He treats the collective as primary.

conscription.rationale: 'Total War' (1943) calls for freeing soldiers for the front and mobilising men and women for war work. He supports compulsory service in war.

media-academia-power.rationale: He describes the press and radio as the 'most influential' instruments for shaping the masses, and says the press creates public opinion. He does not compare these with elected officials.

hereditarian-race.rationale: The 1933 'Racial Question' speech asserts fundamental racial differences in character and creativity, but Wikipedia reports he disparaged 'race-materialism'. Contested, so 0.

organic-representation.rationale: Inferred: The 1933 'Racial Question' speech and 'German Women' say the nation is a community of families and estates rather than of parties and interest groups. Inferred from his rejection of parliamentary parties.

total-state.rationale: 'Total War' (1943) says the state must 'direct every area of life' for the war, and the Reich closes bars, shops and luxury restaurants and reorganises offices and cultural life.

national-rebirth.rationale: His 1933 New Year text calls the year 'German awakening' and says a 'true community of the people' replaced the old decay. He calls for a radical national renewal.

territorial-expansion.rationale: In the 1941 'When or How?' article he says victory would secure 'raw materials, food supplies, living space', and in 1943 'Immortal German Culture' he says the war is about 'our living space'. He supports territorial expansion.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: His Hitler-birthday speeches describe a personal bond between the nation and the Führer, and a 1943 speech says no soldier has broken 'his oath to the Führer'. Authority is tied to personal oaths of loyalty to the leader.

universal-morality.rationale: His 1943 article defends 'the principle of a moral world order' against the enemy, but he applies that morality to the German nation and the Reich. Low, since his morality is national.

single-common-good.rationale: His 1933-1945 texts call for one 'German nation' pursuing one common good and reject the 'insane belief in equality' and party bargaining. He wants a single national interest.

workplace-democracy.rationale: In the 1933 'Racial Question' speech he rejects democracy and majority rule and calls parliamentarianism outdated. He says nothing about votes inside companies, so the answer is low.

force-without-un.rationale: His 1939 and 1941 articles justify the invasions of Poland and the Soviet Union as necessary, with no appeal to any international authority. He endorses force without approval from outside bodies.

reason-over-faith.rationale: His texts speak of 'faith' in the Führer and in the nation's destiny, and he calls for 'the holy seriousness' of national mission. He does not treat reason as the sole guide.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Inferred: He treats welfare and winter relief as service to 'German people, particularly the working people' rather than to all residents. Inferred from the nationalist framing of social provision.

work-for-welfare.rationale: 'Total War' (1943) says the slackers 'must be shaken out of their comfortable ease' and that everyone who can work must do so during the war. He ties entitlement to work.

class-collaboration.rationale: The 1943 speech says 'No class or standing' is exempt from war burdens, and the 1934 New Year text describes a 'true community of the people' replacing class politics.

workers-nation.rationale: The 1943 Sportpalast speech says the workers of the German nation belong to the national community and must serve it, and his 1939 article calls Germany a people's state. He wants workers organised within the nation.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: The 1933 'German Women' speech says 'those things that belong to the man must remain his. That includes politics and the military.' He argues for distinct public roles for men and women.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: The 1933 'Racial Question' speech defends legal action against Jews and the 1941 article calls for their removal from the German community, including from public life. He supported legal racial separation.

national-mission.rationale: His 1941-1945 articles present Germany as the bearer of a European mission against Bolshevism and of the new order for Europe. Partial, and not a claim about spreading a form of government as such.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: The 1933 'German Women' speech says men must keep politics and the military, which is a claim of male-centred order rather than a rejection of it. Low, since he does not describe patriarchy in these terms.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: His articles call the English and American leaders 'plutocrats' and 'corrupt' and the parliamentary parties 'nonsense' and 'mayflies'. He attacks established political elites as out of touch.

night-watchman-state.rationale: He calls for a total state that directs culture, the economy and public life, which is the opposite of a minimal state. He does not limit government to defence and property.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The 1941 'The Jews are Guilty' article says Jews 'have no right to claim equality with us', and the 1933 speech rejects 'the insane belief in equality'. He denies equal moral worth across races and peoples.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: Inferred: His articles describe Germany as encircled by 'plutocratic' and Bolshevik enemies and say the Reich must grow stronger to survive. Inferred from that encirclement framing.

consent-of-governed.rationale: He invokes popular affirmation (the 1933 election and the Sportpalast show of approval) yet rejects parliamentary democracy. The evidence points both ways, so the value is 0.

population-transfer.rationale: The 1941 'The Jews are Guilty' article calls for Jews to be 'removed from the German community' and 'cut out', and the 1938 Nuremberg record shows party leaders were to organise demonstrations against Jewish shops and synagogues. He backed forced removal of a group he regarded as hostile.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Inferred: His texts describe history as a struggle between peoples, in which the strong prevail and the weak perish. Inferred from that conception of struggle.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Inferred: in the 1933 speeches he calls the parties' 'nonsense' outdated and says the Reich now rests on one movement, and his propaganda attacked Communist parties. Inferred from those statements.

separated-powers.rationale: In the 1933 'Racial Question' speech he calls parliamentarianism and the party system outdated and praises a single leadership personality over institutions that debate and check one another.

vanguard-party.rationale: Inferred: He describes the NSDAP as the party that leads the German people and guides the state. Inferred: he sees a movement leading the nation, though not a working-class vanguard.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: The 1933 'Racial Question' speech and the 1941 articles say the Jewish presence splits the German nation and threatens its unity. He treats ethnic difference as a source of conflict.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: He insists on leadership by the Führer and on the 'personality' of leaders, not chance. Low, since the texts do not address lottery selection.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Wikipedia says he promoted the Reichstag Fire Decree and the laws that dismantled democracy after 1933, presenting them as necessary. A secondary report, so low.

party-controls-media.rationale: As Reich Minister he directed the press, radio and film. In the 1933 radio speech he says 'We do not intend to use the radio only for our partisan purposes', and the March 1933 speeches centralise public information under his ministry.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: In his 1943 texts he calls for a Europe 'under Axis leadership' rather than a union of equal nations. Low, since he does not mention the EU or pooling as such.

head-commands-forces.rationale: He calls Hitler the Führer who alone leads the nation and says the war is directed from above, with the leader's will binding the government and armed forces. The head of state, not parliament, commands.

clerical-rule.rationale: He criticises 'Austrian clericalism' and attacks clergy and churches. He does not endorse religious scholars holding political authority.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: His articles call on all Germans to support the war effort and attack defeatism, and he treats opposition to the war as betrayal. He opposes working people undermining their own government in war.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: He organised the 1937 Degenerate Art exhibition and spoke at the 1933 Berlin book burning, which Wikipedia reports, and he attacked works he judged morally harmful. He supports censorship of art on moral grounds.

recall-officials.rationale: Inferred: he dismisses parliamentary politics as the 'nonsense' of parties and praises a leader accountable to the nation rather than to voters' parliaments. Inferred from those statements.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: He promoted the Axis alliance with Italy and Japan and treats the alliances as the basis of German strength. He does not favour ending military alliances.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: His 1933 'German Women' speech says the German village and countryside are part of the nation's healthy core and that the cities' falling birthrate is the sign of decline. Low, since he does not state the claim in those words.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: Wikipedia reports that in 1938 he used propaganda to build support for the Sudeten Germans, and from May 1939 he ran a campaign against Poland. He supported uniting Germans across the Reich's borders.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: His 1941 'The Jews are Guilty' and 1943 articles mock 'tender sensibilities' of educated people and critics. He treats educated critics as out of touch.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: His 1935 Nuremberg speech calls Bolshevism an 'Asiatic-Jewish flood' and his 1941 article calls the Jews 'a parasitic race'. He ranks peoples and cultures as higher or lower.

death-penalty.rationale: 'Total War' (1943) calls for 'draconian penalties' against shirkers and black marketers, and his articles endorse the killing of enemies. He endorses severe state punishment, though not the death penalty as a named policy.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: He required proof of 'Aryan descent' for journalists in the 1933 press law, and the regime's citizenship rules tie membership to German blood. He favours citizenship by descent.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: 'More Morality, Less Moralism' (1934) mocks moralists who police personal conduct, dress and female behaviour, and argues for private freedom. Only partial support, so low.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Inferred: He argues that the press's freedom must find limits where it conflicts with the people and the state, and that the state must guide the economy. Inferred from those statements.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: In 1939 he says the state's social principles serve the whole people and attacks rich 'City men' who keep wealth from others. No clear statement on property rights.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Wikipedia reports he backed the 1938 annexation of the Sudeten territory as a return to the Reich. He treated annexations as legitimate.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Wikipedia reports that in February 1937 he said he wanted to eliminate the Protestant Church and attacked the Catholic Church in 1937. A secondary report, so low.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Inferred: He presents Hitler as standing above the parties, 'the Führer', and as the embodiment of the national will. Inferred from that presentation.

sacred-ruler.rationale: He calls the Führer a 'blessed man' with a 'divine gift' for leadership and says history made him leader. Low, since he does not say the ruler is of divine descent.

character-from-environment.rationale: The 1933 'Racial Question' speech and the 1941 articles describe the Jews and others as innately destructive or creative by race, which downplays upbringing as the main cause of character.

leader-cult.rationale: His annual 'Our Hitler' speeches from 1933 to 1945 praise the Führer as the embodiment of the nation in mass rallies and public homage. He actively promoted the leader cult.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Wikipedia reports that he used propaganda for the Sudeten Germans in 1938, a claim justified by the German population there. He supported territorial claims on the basis of national populations.

women-must-cover.rationale: In 1934 he ridicules moralists who would limit women's smoking, bobbed hair and public life, calling such rules out of place in a modern cultural state. He does not address covering clothing directly.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: His 1941-1945 articles present German-led Europe as saving the continent from Bolshevism and Jewish-led chaos, and describe Eastern peoples as inferior. Low, since he does not use the term tutelage.

patriotic-education.rationale: 'Youth and the War' (1940) describes Hitler Youth and League of German Girls education as forming loyal young Germans who imitate the Führer. He wants youth formed in loyalty to the nation.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: He backed racial exclusion of Jews from public life and treated racial standing as central to national life. Low, since he did not address affirmative action.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: Inferred: he backed the exclusion of Jews from economic life and the counter-boycott of Jewish shops, which permitted private refusal of service on racial grounds. Inferred from his support for that exclusion.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: In the 1933 speeches he argues that majority-rule democracy and its checks are outdated. No statement on a written bill of rights.

parliament-supreme.rationale: He calls parliamentarianism and the party system 'outdated concepts' for Germany (1933) and mocks parliamentary politics as the 'nonsense' of party interests.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: 'Total War' (1943) says 'Rich and poor, high and low must share the burdens equally', which casts the privileged as bound to bear their share for the community.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: The 1939 'The Coffee Drinkers' article says Germany must cover its needs from its own resources. This is autarky, not a judgment on aid to poor countries.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Wikipedia reports his 1938 propaganda for the Sudeten Germans, who were part of Czechoslovakia after the 1919 settlement. He supported recovering territory lost in the peace settlement.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: He attacks the anti-Nazi left and calls the opposition to his state a plot of 'Marxist' and 'Jewish' enemies, so he rejects anti-fascism as a founding value.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: He rejects the claim that National Socialism and Bolshevism are similar, arguing that National Socialism is a German phenomenon that opposes Bolshevism's terror. He does not treat them as equal.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Inferred: In the 1933 'Racial Question' speech he quotes Mussolini that Fascism 'is not for export' and says National Socialism is 'a completely German phenomenon'. Inferred: political forms belong to a people.

paid-care-work.rationale: In 'Total War' (1943) he asks women with household help whether they need it, and wants women to work in war industry rather than in domestic service. Low, since he does not discuss paid care directly.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Inferred: he rejects parliamentary accountability and praises a leader whose authority rests on the nation's will rather than the instructions of electors. Inferred from those statements.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Inferred: in the 1933 speeches he treats parliamentary budgeting as one of the 'parliamentary intrigues' the new government ends. Inferred from that rejection.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: 'Total War' (1943) calls beauty shops and fashion salons 'a waste of time during war' and closes luxury outlets. This is a wartime judgment, not a general view of consumption.

corporate-influence.rationale: He attacks 'plutocratic' power in Britain and the United States and says the press serves plutocratic democracy. He does not discuss corporate lobbying in general.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: The 1933 'German Women' speech calls for special attention to families with many children and demands that the state halt the decline in births. He backs incentives to raise the birthrate.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: The 1941 'The Jews are Guilty' article says 'Every Jew is our enemy' and that 'all Jews... are part of an international conspiracy against National Socialist Germany'. He directly asserts the conspiracy claim.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: The 1945 'The Creators of the World's Misfortunes' article says 'Capitalism and Bolshevism have the same Jewish roots' and treats capitalist power as a force of domination. He does not regard capitalism as progressive.

holocaust-denial.rationale: In 'The War and the Jews' (1943) he writes that the 'wiping out of the Jewish race' is a process that 'can no longer be halted'. He affirmed rather than denied the destruction of Europe's Jews.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Wikipedia reports the 1933 disbanding of trade unions and his speeches treat political opposition as enemy action, including the Communist threat he campaigned against. He backed suppression of opposition.

participatory-democracy.rationale: He says 'the people want to be led' and describes decisions as made by the Führer on the nation's behalf, not by participatory bodies in workplaces and communities.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Inferred: he describes the Führer's leadership as a 'divine gift' and invokes the Almighty over the nation's destiny, which implies authority above the people's will. Inferred from those statements.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: In 'England's Guilt' (1939) he says 'the press, which serves plutocratic democracy' brands critics of the social order as rascals. He links press control to wealth.

racial-franchise.rationale: The 1941 'The Jews are Guilty' article says Jews 'have no right to a voice in the community' and the 1933 speech ties political standing to racial identity. He would limit political voice by race.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: The 1939 'England's Guilt' article says British 'lords and City men' are the richest people on earth while the masses are impoverished and the press serves plutocracy. He treats concentrated wealth as a threat to the people.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: He attacks Bolshevik atheism and the Marxist campaign to 'destroy' religion, and he treats faith as part of national life. He does not endorse a state campaign for atheism.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: He treats order and security as the state's first duty and calls for 'draconian penalties' in 'Total War' (1943). He does not regard abolishing police and prisons as acceptable.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: He rejects sharing power with the Jews and other groups he calls enemies, and his articles describe divided societies as needing a single national leadership.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: The 1933 'German Women' speech says 'the man' must keep his leading role in life and politics, and that the family is for the woman's motherhood. Marriage authority is not discussed directly.

uniformed-youth.rationale: 'Youth and the War' (1940) praises the Hitler Youth and the League of German Girls for national service and discipline, and says the youth must learn respect for 'sacrificial manhood'.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: His articles and 'Total War' justify killing in war and call for the total defeat of enemies. He does not regard killing as never justified.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: The 1943 Sportpalast speech says 'I shall remember the heroes of Stalingrad, who put me and all of us under a deep obligation', and he honours the fallen as examples. He honours those who die for the nation.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: Inferred: he frames the war as a struggle against 'infernal' forces and the 'devilish' enemy, and the 1943 'The War and the Jews' describes a moral world order at stake. Inferred from that framing.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: The 1941 'The Jews are Guilty' article calls for removing Jews from the German community, and the 1943 'The War and the Jews' says Jews organise the enemy's war economy. He wants the economy in the hands of the German majority.

independent-unions.rationale: Wikipedia reports that unions were disbanded in 1933 and replaced by the German Labour Front. He is not recorded defending unions independent of the state.

family-wage.rationale: The 1933 'German Women' speech puts the family at the centre of the nation and gives men the leading role in life and politics. No explicit wage statement.

person-over-state.rationale: He subordinates individuals to the national community and treats the Jews as to be removed from it. He does not regard the state as existing to serve the person.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Inferred: his speeches present politics as serving the nation's 'soul' and spiritual forces as well as material interests. Inferred from those statements.

racial-group-interests.rationale: The 1933 'Racial Question' speech says the Jews and the German nation have distinct racial interests and that the racial problem must be solved for the nation's security. He treats racial groups as having political interests.

racial-pride.rationale: The 1933 'Racial Question' speech says 'no people with any self esteem could tolerate' the condition of Germany and describes the Aryan as a 'creative creature'. He treats racial pride as legitimate.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: 'Total War' (1943) presents the attack on the Soviet Union as a necessary answer to a threat, and calls for the 'most radical' measures. He does not confine armed forces to defence.

foreign-partition-plot.rationale: The 1945 'Creators of the World's Misfortunes' article and the 1943 'Clay Giant' article say Roosevelt and Churchill plan an occupation of Germany that would destroy and exterminate its people. He says foreign powers plot to dismember Germany.

women-distinct-values.rationale: The 1933 'German Women' speech says women have a 'different mission, a different value' from men, centred on motherhood and care. He values women's distinct role without giving them weight in public policy.

arms-reduction.rationale: He demands rearmament and total war, and treats Germany's military strength as a precondition of its survival. Low, since no direct statement against arms reduction appears in the texts read.

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: His texts call on soldiers and the home front to fight and sacrifice, and 'The Call of Duty' (1944) treats opposition to the war as betrayal. He does not endorse refusal to fight.

sacred-nation.rationale: The 1933 'German Women' speech says the women's motherhood guarantees 'the immortality of the nation', and his speeches treat the nation as a community that outlasts its members. He calls the nation sacred.

shared-human-nature.rationale: He says the 'human nature' of the Jews and of other peoples differs by race and that the Jewish 'parasitic' nature must be removed. He does not regard a shared human nature as a basis for equal rights.

public-service-media.rationale: In 1933 he calls radio 'the most crucial instrument... for influencing the masses' and says the Ministry will use it for its own purposes. He did not favour media free of government control.

workers-own-party.rationale: He drove the one-party state and called the party system outdated (1933). He did not support working people's own independent party.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: He cites the 1933 free election that gave Hitler power as legitimating, yet calls parliamentary democracy and majority rule outdated. Contested, so 0.

women-suffrage.rationale: The 1933 'German Women' speech says the right to be elected to office 'at the expense of the right to life, motherhood, and her daily bread' is a bad trade. He opposes women holding public office as a matter of principle.

race-social-construct.rationale: The 1933 'Racial Question' speech describes race as founded in human nature and as shaping whole peoples' conduct. Wikipedia says he disparaged 'race-materialism', so the position is contested and low.

gender-equality-agencies.rationale: The 1933 'German Women' speech says the state should rebuild women's family role and does not see equality agencies as necessary. Low, because the texts do not address agencies directly.

simple-living.rationale: 'Total War' (1943) says Germans are 'voluntarily giving up a significant part of our living standard' and closes luxury shops and restaurants. This is wartime austerity, not a general ideal of simple living.

homeland-spiritual-bond.rationale: In 'Total War' he speaks of defending 'their families, women and children, the beautiful and untouched countryside, their cities and villages' and their two-thousand-year culture. He treats the homeland as a sacred bond.

protect-kin-minorities.rationale: Wikipedia reports that in 1938 he used propaganda to build support for the Sudeten Germans, a German minority in Czechoslovakia. He supported action on behalf of co-nationals abroad.

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: In 1933 he says the parties 'carried on their nonsense in the parliaments' and that the Führer's movement now governs without them. He wanted parties and interest groups bypassed.

national-resource-control.rationale: In 'The Coffee Drinkers' (1939) he says Germany cannot cover its needs without colonies, so control of raw materials matters to him. No direct statement on foreign control.

patriotism-serves-workers.rationale: His texts present National Socialism as serving 'the working people' and the 1939 article calls Germany 'a socialist people's state'. He pairs national loyalty with service to workers.

notes: Changes of view: in 1925-1926 he wrote anti-capitalist and socialist-leaning texts, then aligned fully with Hitler after 1926; the later record is used throughout. Sources for speeches are translations held by the German Propaganda Archive; the Kristallnacht evidence is a secondhand Nuremberg summary of his remarks. The 1920s German original texts and the full diaries were not read. Several answers rest on Wikipedia, a secondary source, and are marked low or medium for that reason. Positions on the Sportpalast speech are taken from the full translated text. Inferred answers are marked low with 'Inferred:' in the rationale.
